newsitem.title: USA: Euthanasia increases in the Netherlands - study.
newsitem.headline: Euthanasia increases in the Netherlands - study.

text.p: The numbers of cases of euthanasia and physician-assisted suicide are rising in the Netherlands even though both practices are technically illegal, according to a report to be published on Thursday.

The study, reported in the New England Journal of Medicine by a team led by Dr. Paul van der Maas of Erasmus University in Rotterdam, was part of an effort to see if tacit legalization of both procedures would open the door to deaths for morally unacceptable reasons.

"A major issue in the debate about euthanasia is whether some form of acceptance of euthanasia or assisted suicide when it is explicitly requested by a greatly suffering, terminally ill, competent patient is the first step in a slippery slope (leading to casual killing of the sick)," they said.

"In our view, these data do not support the idea that physicians in the Netherlands are moving down a slippery slope," they said, because "there are no signs that the decision making has become less careful."

Using a 1991 study as their basis, the team polled more than 400 physicians and studied more than 6,000 death records to see if the rate at which doctors were helping people die had increased over five years. They found that it had.

But in an editorial accompanying the report, Journal executive editor Marcia Angell said the studies showed that doctors were in no rush to perform euthanasia or physician-assisted suicides. They did it for fewer than a third of the people who requested it, she wrote. Eighty seven percent of the recipients were expected to die within a week, 12 percent in a month.

Euthanasia cases accounted for 1.8 percent of the deaths in the 1991 study, rising to about 2.4 percent in 1996. Physician-assisted suicide rose from 0.3 percent to 0.4 percent. The Dutch make little distinction between the two.

Of the doctors surveyed, 53 percent confirmed that they had performed euthanasia or assisted in suicide and 29 percent confirmed they had done so in the previous 24 months. In contrast, the van der Maas team documented a decline in the number of incidents of euthanasia carried out without the explicit immediate request of the patient.
In the 1991 study, 0.8 percent of the patients were killed without a concurrent request from the patient, compared to 0.7 percent in the latest study.
